title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 50
paragraphs: So it is because these named rivers and many others join their waters together that the Ister becomes the greatest of rivers; for if we compare single streams, the Nile is superior in volume of water, since no river or spring flows into it to contribute to its volume. The Ister flows at an equal level always, both in summer and winter, for some such reason as this, I suppose. In winter it is at its natural size, or becomes only a little larger than usual, since this land receives very little rain in winter but constantly has snow; whereas in summer the snow that fell in winter, being abundant, melts and runs from all parts into the Ister. This snow, running into the river, helps to swell its volume, and with it also many violent showers of rain—for it rains during summer. Thus the waters mingling with the Ister are more copious in summer than in winter by roughly as much as the water the sun draws to himself in summer exceeds what he draws in winter. By the setting of these things against one another, a balance is produced, so that the river is seen to be of equal volume always.
